reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline variants in the FLCN (folliculin) tumour suppressor gene, inherited autosomal dominantly
Classic triad of features involves the skin, lungs, and kidneys, though not all are present in every patient
Characteristic cutaneous lesions are fibrofolliculomas and trichodiscomas, typically small dome-shaped papules on the face, neck, and upper trunk appearing in adulthood
Multiple pulmonary cysts, predominantly basal and peripheral, predispose to recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax
Confers an increased risk of renal tumours that are often bilateral and multifocal, with chromophobe and hybrid oncocytic histologies being characteristic
Renal imaging surveillance is central to management to detect and manage tumours early, favouring nephron-sparing approaches
Patients should be counselled about pneumothorax risk, including avoidance of high-risk activities and awareness of relevant precautions
Recognition of the skin lesions or unexplained pneumothorax can be the entry point to diagnosis and cascade family testing
reference.pathophysiology: FLCN encodes folliculin, a tumour suppressor that interacts with the AMPK and mTOR signalling networks to regulate cell growth, energy metabolism, and autophagy. Loss of folliculin function disturbs these pathways in a tissue-specific manner, producing benign follicular skin tumours, weakening of alveolar architecture that generates lung cysts and predisposes to pneumothorax, and dysregulated proliferation of renal tubular cells that drives multifocal renal tumours.
additionalDifferentials: Von Hippel-Lindau disease (renal tumours and cysts)
Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer
Tuberous sclerosis complex (renal and pulmonary manifestations)
Sporadic multiple facial papules or spontaneous pneumothorax
additionalInvestigations: Germline FLCN sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis with genetic counselling
Renal imaging surveillance, favouring MRI to limit cumulative radiation over long-term follow-up
Dermatological assessment and, where needed, skin biopsy of characteristic lesions
Chest imaging to characterise pulmonary cysts in those with respiratory symptoms or pneumothorax
Assessment and counselling regarding pneumothorax risk
redFlags: Growing or bilateral renal mass reaching the threshold for intervention
Family history of renal tumours or pneumothorax in a patient with characteristic skin lesions
New respiratory distress suggesting acute pneumothorax in a known carrier
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good with surveillance, as many renal tumours are indolent and amenable to nephron-sparing treatment, and pneumothoraces are manageable. Outcome depends on early detection of renal tumours and appropriate handling of recurrent pneumothorax, with lifelong renal follow-up recommended.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent pneumothorax without recognising the underlying syndrome
Attributing facial papules to acne or other benign conditions and missing the diagnosis
Choosing radical rather than nephron-sparing surgery for multifocal renal tumours
Relying on repeated CT surveillance and accumulating unnecessary radiation exposure over decades
management: Regular renal imaging surveillance, favouring MRI to limit cumulative radiation, to detect multifocal renal tumours early
Nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy for renal tumours where feasible, preserving renal function
Counsel on pneumothorax risk and manage recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax, considering pleurodesis for recurrent episodes
Treat troublesome fibrofolliculomas cosmetically with laser ablation or excision as needed
Confirm the diagnosis with germline FLCN sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis alongside genetic counselling
Offer cascade testing to at-risk relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance, with lifelong renal follow-up
